newsitem.title: INDIA: India copper firm sees no end to woes from budget.
newsitem.headline: India copper firm sees no end to woes from budget.

text.p: India's decision to cut import duty on copper concentrates has given no immediate relief to Hindustan Copper Ltd (HCL) but would help as the firm expands smelter capacity, officials and analysts said on Monday.
Starved for cash, the state-owned HCL has been looking to tax reliefs from the government.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his 1997/98 (April-March) budget, presented to parliament in February, cut customs duty on copper concentrates to five percent from 10 percent but made no changes in tariffs on the metal and products.
As a result HCL's raw material would become cheaper if it imports concentrates, but the firm is not importing right now.
On the other hand, HCL did not get the tariff protection on its final product that it was looking for.
HCL had urged the government to raise import duties on copper products to offset a cash crunch resulting from high production costs and a steep fall in London metal prices.
"We stand at the same place. There is no change in customs tariffs," a senior HCL official told Reuters.
The company in a letter to the Mines Ministry had demanded that customs duty be raised to 60 percent from 30 percent for copper cathodes and wire bars and to 65 percent for wire rods.
HCL, India's sole primary copper producer, has a production capacity for 47,500 tonnes of refined copper and currently operates its mines and plants at full capacity.
Analysts say the copper content in Indian ore is very poor, leading to higher costs. HCL officials say profits have been eroded as the firm has had to cut prices to match imports.
"We will not get any immediate benefits from changes in import duties on copper concentrates because we are not importing any concentrates," said the HCL official, who did not want to be identified.

The official said HCL would benefit when it expanded its copper smelter and refinery at Khetri in the northwestern state of Rajasthan to 100,000 tonnes from 31,000 tonnes at a cost of nearly 5.3 billion rupees ($148 million).
Officials said HCL will use imported copper concentrates for its expanded capacity.
"The move (import duty cut) will benefit companies like Sterlite Industries, which imports concentrates," said Prakash Patra of investment firm Peregrine Securities.
Patra said there was no case for increasing customs duties, as demanded by HCL, when duties on other products were being brought down in line with global trends.
Company officials said the Khetri project was expected to be commissioned by the end of 1998 and it was likely to earn an additional profit of 1.6 billion rupees annually.
India's Mines Ministry said government approval for the expansion of the Khetri complex was at an advanced stage.
"The reduction in customs duty on copper concentrates from 10 to five percent will have a definitive impact on the profitability of HCL," the ministry said in a statement.
"Two stages have been completed and a third stage clearance was coming up later this month. It will then go to the cabinet," said the HCL official.
HCL's loss in 1996/97 (April-March) was expected to be substantial. Despite cost-cutting, HCL had up to December 1996 nearly one billion rupees, company officials said.
The landed cost of imported copper depends on copper prices on the London Metal Exchange (LME), prevailing customs duty rates and the rupee-dollar exchange rate.
Officials said in the past few months the LME price of copper fell by $600 per tonne compared to prices that prevailed at the corresponding period of the previous year.
